Shalini had printed the competition rulebook and was underlining it with a red pen. "Robot must fit in a 30 cm box. Event date: 14 December." Ramesh drew a line across the whiteboard and wrote 14 Dec at the far right. Then he worked leftwards, thinking aloud. "Last week, nothing. Just rest and pack. So we stop on the 7th. Rehearsal before that, one week. Testing, two weeks. Build, three." Shalini counted on her fingers. "That puts design at... now. Like, this week." They both went quiet and looked at the calendar. Then Ramesh circled the date in red. I can't say what they were feeling, but they packed up faster than I've ever seen.

2 August. Avni read the rules aloud in the school library while Tanuja wrote: "Weight limit 2 kg. Design report due 20 September. Event: 5 October." Avni frowned. "If we want a free week at the end, we have to be finished by 28 September. And the report is due before we've even tested it." They worked backward on graph paper: design by 20 August, build by 10 September, testing till the 28th.
9 September. The gearbox had cracked twice. Tanuja checked the sheet. "Build ends tomorrow. We print the spare part tonight, or testing starts late." They stayed an extra hour.
30 September. While other teams rewired frantically in the corridor, Avni and Tanuja packed their robot into its box and went to buy samosas. Tanuja grinned. "I didn't know a free week felt this good."

After ten minutes Thomas drew a table on the back of an old calendar: cost, time, our skill. Each idea got a score from one to three in each column. The drone scored high on excitement and one on everything else. The hovercraft lost on cost. "The line-follower's boring," Sunaina said, "but it wins every column." Thomas stared at it. "Unless we make it less boring. What if we put the sensors in a curve, not a straight row? It'd see turns earlier." Sunaina grinned and wrote that on a twenty-first note.

passage:
Robotics coach's notes, week 6.
Suraj and Reena set up the mock track in the corridor after school and ran the robot fifty times. Reena kept the log in a ruled notebook: run number, where it failed, what they thought caused it. By run twenty Suraj wanted to stop and "just fix everything," but Reena kept going. When they totalled it, 19 of the 50 runs had failed. Eleven failures were at the curve under the corridor window, where sunlight hit the track and the sensor lost the line. Five were a wheel slipping; three were a low battery. They taped a small cardboard hood over the sensor first, since that was the biggest problem. The next twenty runs had two failures.
What I did next: I moved the mock track to a spot that gets strong afternoon sun on purpose, so they can test the fix in the worst light.

qa.a: 19 of the 50 runs had failed.

qa.q: How was Suraj feeling around run twenty?
qa.a: Suraj felt impatient and wanted to stop and just fix everything, while Reena kept going.

qa.q: What should they fix after the sensor hood, and why?
qa.a: The slipping wheel, since it caused the next most failures; then another round of runs will show what remains.

qa.q: How might Reena see the log after they totalled it?
qa.a: Reena likely feels vindicated, since the notebook showed the sunny curve caused most failures and gave them a clear first fix.

grounding: Shows students running a robot fifty times on a mock track, logging each failure and cause, and fixing the most frequent problem, sensor glare, first.

Fifty runs today on the practice mat in Joseph's garage. My arm aches from resetting the robot. Joseph thought it was pointless ("it works, Urmi, we've seen it work"), but I made him call out each failure while I wrote it down.
Tally by 6 pm:
left wheel wobbling off: 9
missed the black line at the sharp turn: 4
stopped for no reason: 2

Joseph tightened the grub screw and added a drop of glue. We ran ten more before his mum called us for dinner: zero wheel falls. 😊
Tomorrow: the sharp turn.
Urmila

passage: You want to know how three of us built a sorting robot in eight weeks without a single big fight? Honestly, it was the roles. I'm Yamini, I'm the talker, so I took the documentation and the presentation. Hrithik has hands like a watch-repairer, so the wiring was his. Fatima writes code the way I write messages, fast and neat, so she took the program. But here's what we did right: every Saturday morning we met for one hour, and each person had to explain their part to the other two. I learned what a pull-up resistor is. Hrithik learned why judges care about a clean diagram. When Fatima was down with fever before the demo, Hrithik and I could still run the code and explain it. Splitting the work is good. Splitting the understanding is not.

Looking back, one run on a straight line wasn't a test at all.

Mentor's note, Saturday evening, after round one.
Chetan and Kashish arrived this morning looking tired and oddly proud. They told me they'd added an obstacle-avoid feature last night "for bonus points." I asked whether they had tested it. Chetan said, "Twice. In the hostel corridor." The arena has a shiny floor and bright lights. In round one the robot kept seeing obstacles that weren't there, stopping and turning in circles, and they scored eleven out of forty. Kashish sat on the bench with her head in her hands.
What I did next: I asked them to roll back to Thursday's tested code for round two, and they scored thirty-one. Then we sat down together and wrote a rule on the first page of their notebook: no new features in the last three days, only fixes tested on the real track.

Friday, 9 pm
Today was the district science fair and it was a disaster.
Nilesh built our whole solar tracker himself over the last month. Whenever I offered to help, he said, "It's faster if I do it, Lakshmi." It was faster. So Farhan and I made the poster, and that's all.
This morning his mother called: Nilesh had a high fever and wasn't coming. Farhan and I stood next to a machine we had never switched on. The first judge asked why the panel turns toward the light. I said, "Because of the sensors?" She asked, "Which sensors?" I didn't know. Farhan tried to start it and pressed the wrong switch. The panel just sat there.
I'm not even angry at Nilesh. I'm angry at us for letting it happen. Next project, everyone learns everything, at least once.
Lakshmi

Two weeks before. Amandeep spread the robot's parts on the floor and asked Disha, "What could break on the day?" They listed it: the battery, the ultrasonic sensor, the loose wheel, the USB cable. "Then we carry one of each," Amandeep said. "And one of us only fixes." Disha volunteered.

At the bottom Bidisha wrote "Next year," and Pradeep, grudgingly, added the first line: calibrate at the venue during setup. Then a second: book practice slots from August.

passage: The science teacher at the zilla parishad school in Wardha had borrowed a stopwatch from the PT teacher. Avni and Tanuja stood beside their water-level alarm while their parents sat on the front bench. "Three minutes. Go." Avni began with the problem: farmers walking to the tank at night to check the water. Tanuja showed the float sensor. At three minutes ten, the stopwatch beeped. Tanuja's father raised his hand. "If it's in the tank, won't it give a shock?" Avni hesitated. They had never heard it asked that way. The teacher wrote it on the board, with Avni's mother's question: "How much would one cost a farmer?" That evening the two girls shortened the middle part and wrote two answers on a card: the circuit runs on a small battery sealed in a plastic box, and the parts cost about 450 rupees. The next rehearsal took two minutes fifty.
